chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, all from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Jameel, from Zurara, from Abu Basir, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
Humran asked him, 'May Allah make me a ransom for you! If you were to narrate to us when this Matter will occur, it would make us happy.'

He said, 'O Humran! You have friends, brothers, and acquaintances. There was a scholar in the past who had a son who was not interested in his father's knowledge and did not ask him about anything. He had a neighbor who would come to him, ask him, and take knowledge from him. When death approached the man, he called his son and said, 'O my son! You have shown disinterest in what I have, your desire for it is low, and you never asked me about anything. I have a neighbor who used to come to me, ask me, take from me, and memorize from me. So if you need anything, go to him.' He introduced his neighbor to him. The man died, and his son remained.

The king of that era saw a dream and asked about the man. It was said to him, 'He has died.' The king said, 'Did he leave a son?' It was said, 'Yes, he left a son.' The king said, 'Bring him to me.' They were sent to him to bring him to the king. The boy said, 'By Allah, I do not know why the king is calling me, and I have no knowledge. If he asks me about something, I will be disgraced.' He remembered what his father had bequeathed to him, so he went to the man who used to take knowledge from his father. He said to him, 'The king has sent for me to ask me, and I do not know what he has sent for me. My father had ordered me to come to you if I needed anything.'

The man said, 'But I know what he has sent for you. If I inform you, then whatever Allah brings out to you, it will be between you and me.' He said, 'Yes.' He took an oath from him and made a binding agreement that he would be loyal. The boy made a binding agreement with him. He said, 'He wants to ask you about a dream he saw, as to which era it is. So say to him, 'This is the era of the wolf.''

The boy went to him. The king said to him, 'Do you know why I sent for you?' He said, 'You sent for me intending to ask me about a dream you saw, as to which era it is.' The king said, 'You speak the truth, so inform me which era this is.' He said to him, 'The era of the wolf.' So he ordered an award for him, and the boy took it and returned to his house. He refused to be loyal to his companion.

He said, 'Perhaps I will not exhaust this wealth, nor consume it until I die, and perhaps I will not need him, nor be asked about something like this which I was asked about.' So he remained for as long as Allah willed.

Then the king saw a dream and sent for him, calling him. He regretted what he had done and said, 'By Allah, I have no knowledge to give him, and I do not know how to deal with my companion, and I have betrayed him and not been loyal to him.' Then he said, 'I will go to him in any case, and I will excuse myself to him, and I will swear to him, perhaps he will inform me.' So he went to him and said, 'I have done what I have done, and I have not been loyal to you for what was between us, and what was in my hand has gone, and I have need of you. So I adjure you by Allah not to abandon me, and I make a binding agreement with you that nothing will be given to me except that it will be between you and me. The king has sent for me, and I do not know what he will ask me about.'
He said, 'He wants to ask you about a dream he saw, as to which era it is. So say to him, 'This is the era of the ram.''

He went to the king and entered upon him. The king said, 'Why did I send for you?' He said, 'You saw a dream and you want to ask me which era this is.' The king said to him, 'You speak the truth, so inform me which era this is.' He said, 'This is the era of the ram.' So he ordered a gift for him, and he took it and returned to his house. He pondered in his mind whether to be loyal to his companion or not. Sometimes he thought to do it, and sometimes he thought not to do it. Then he said, 'Perhaps I will not need him after this time ever,' and he decided on betrayal and leaving loyalty. So he remained for as long as Allah willed.

Then the king saw a dream and sent for him. He regretted what he had done between himself and his companion and said, 'After betraying him twice, how shall I act, and I have no knowledge?' Then he decided on going to the man. He went to him and adjured him by Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and asked him to teach him, and informed him that this time he would be loyal to him and made a binding agreement with him, saying, 'Do not leave me in this state, for I will not return to betrayal, and I will be loyal to you.' He made a binding agreement with him. He said, 'He is calling you to ask you about a dream he saw, as to which era it is. When he asks you, inform him that it is the era of the scale.'

He said, 'So he went to the king and entered upon him. The king said to him, 'Why did I send for you?' He said, 'You saw a dream and you want to ask me which era this is.' He said, 'You speak the truth, so inform me which era this is.' He said, 'This is the era of the scale.' So he ordered a gift for him, and he took it and went with it to the man. He placed it before him and said, 'I have come to you with what was given to me, so divide it with me.''

The scholar said to him, 'The first era was the era of the wolf, and you were from the wolves. The second era was the era of the ram, which thinks but does not act, and so you were thinking but not being loyal. This era was the era of the scale, and you were upon loyalty. So take your wealth, for I have no need for it,' and he returned it to him.
ai.seo_question: What is the story of the scholar's son and the three eras in Kafi?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Baqir (as) uses the parable of the scholar's son to illustrate the spiritual states of the community across three eras: the 'Era of the Wolf' (aggression), the 'Era of the Ram' (hesitation), and the 'Era of the Scale' (balance and fidelity). The son’s progression from betrayal to loyalty mirrors the expected conduct of the faithful, emphasizing that true success lies in maintaining trust (*amanah*) and fulfilling covenants with knowledge bearers.
